x_title: Radial Acceleration Relation in Rotationally Supported Galaxies
x_claim: McGaugh et al. show that a universal radial acceleration relation exists across 153 rotationally supported galaxies, in which the total acceleration (including the dark matter contribution) is fully specified by the baryonic acceleration, constituting a natural law for rotating galaxies.

y_title: Novel Test of Modified Newtonian Dynamics with Gas Rich Galaxies
y_claim: McGaugh shows that gas-rich galaxies fall precisely on the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation with scatter attributable entirely to observational uncertainty, consistent with a single effective force law governing galaxy dynamics.
y_evidence: The data fall precisely where predicted a priori by the modified Newtonian dynamics. The scatter in the BTFR is attributable entirely to observational uncertainty, consistent with a single effective force law.
conjunction: McGaugh and collaborators have established universal scaling relations in galaxy dynamics—the radial acceleration relation across 153 galaxies [x] and the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation in gas-rich galaxies [y]—showing that the total dynamical mass is fully specified by baryons, consistent with a single effective force law.
conjunction_anon: McGaugh and collaborators have established universal scaling relations in galaxy dynamics—the radial acceleration relation across 153 galaxies [A] and the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation in gas-rich galaxies [B]—showing that the total dynamical mass is fully specified by baryons, consistent with a single effective force law.
x_background: The observed acceleration g_obs = v²/r is computed from rotation curves using Newtonian kinematics, and the baryonic acceleration g_bar is computed from the observed baryon distribution using Newtonian gravity; the residual (g_obs − g_bar) is attributed to dark matter, and the tight correlation between g_obs and g_bar is an empirical regularity within this Newtonian-plus-dark-matter framework.
y_background: Below the characteristic acceleration a0, Newtonian dynamics break down and galaxy dynamics are governed by a single modified force law, so the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation follows directly from this modified force law rather than from Newtonian gravity plus dark matter.
why_conflict: P2 asserts that Newtonian dynamics hold at very low accelerations, requiring dark matter to explain the mass discrepancy. Q2 asserts that Newtonian dynamics break down below a0, so the same discrepancy reflects modified gravity with no need for dark matter. The two positions on whether Newtonian dynamics are valid at low accelerations are mutually exclusive.
orphan_conclusion: Dark matter in galaxies follows a single effective force law, as evidenced by both the radial acceleration relation and the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation.
llm_notes: Both papers are by McGaugh, who uses empirical scaling relations to probe the dark-matter-vs-MOND tension. Paper x operates within the Lambda-CDM framework: it explicitly references dark matter dominating at large radii and decomposes acceleration into baryonic and dark matter components using Newtonian dynamics (P2). Paper y explicitly frames its result as a test of MOND and concludes consistency with 'a single effective force law,' directly invoking Q2. A literature-review writer combining these without flagging the theoretical tension would implicitly suggest that dark matter behaves as if governed by a modified force law—a claim Lambda-CDM rejects (the RAR emerges from galaxy formation/feedback, not a force law) and MOND also rejects (there is no dark matter). Human verifier should confirm that the RAR paper's use of Newtonian dynamics to compute both g_obs and g_bar constitutes a genuine dependence on P2 rather than a purely kinematic measurement independent of dynamical theory.

The orphan conclusion—that both mechanisms jointly explain rotation curves—is rejected by both frameworks: Lambda-CDM attributes rotation curves to dark matter under Newtonian gravity alone, and MOND attributes them to modified dynamics alone.
